ultrafast-001.question: Which correctly describes the mode-locked state of the many longitudinal modes oscillating in a laser cavity?
choices: Even with random phases, light becomes a regular pulse train if there are enough modes, and the pulse duration is set by the round-trip time
The laser is restricted to a single longitudinal mode, and a modulator outside the cavity varies its intensity with the round-trip period to make short pulses
The phases of the equally spaced modes are locked, so they add up into a pulse every round trip, about as short as the inverse of the total bandwidth
ultrafast-001.explanation: When the phases of N longitudinal modes spaced by Δf = c/(2L) are aligned, the fields of all modes add up together at certain times and cancel at others, giving a pulse train with period 1/Δf (the round-trip time). The pulse duration is about 1/(NΔf), the inverse of the total bandwidth of the locked modes. With random phases the intensity just fluctuates irregularly, the same as continuous light on average, and no regular pulse train forms. Varying the intensity of one mode is intensity modulation; its spectrum is narrow, so fs pulses cannot be obtained. In mode locking, the more modes are aligned, the shorter the pulse.

ultrafast-002.question: In passive mode locking with a saturable absorber, why does a short pulse build up on its own?
choices: A saturable absorber absorbs more as the light gets stronger, so peaks are clipped and the pulse widens each round trip until it finally settles at a fixed width
A saturable absorber absorbs less as the light gets stronger, so intense peaks see lower loss, and over repeated round trips a strong, short pulse is selected
An external high-frequency electrical signal applied to the saturable absorber forces its loss to vary with the same period as the cavity round-trip time, carving out the pulse
ultrafast-002.explanation: In a saturable absorber, strong light empties the lower level of the absorption so the absorption saturates and the loss drops. If the light intensity in the cavity has a small fluctuation, its peak sees little loss while the wings and weaker parts see large loss, so with each round trip the peak alone grows stronger and narrower in time. Semiconductor saturable absorber mirrors (SESAMs) are used, and Ti:sapphire lasers use an extremely fast effective saturable absorber formed by Kerr self-focusing combined with an aperture (Kerr-lens mode locking). Absorption that increases with intensity is the property of an optical limiter. Varying the loss with an external signal is active mode locking; passive mode locking uses no external signal.

ultrafast-003.question: Which is closest to the peak power of the pulses from a mode-locked laser with an average power of 1 W, a repetition rate of 100 MHz and a pulse duration of 100 fs? (Treat the pulse as a rectangle 100 fs wide.)
choices: About 100 kW
About 1 W
About 10 µW
ultrafast-003.explanation: The energy per pulse is the average power divided by the repetition rate, 1 W / (100×10⁶ Hz) = 10 nJ. Concentrated into 100 fs, this gives a peak power of 10×10⁻⁹ J / 100×10⁻¹⁵ s = 1×10⁵ W, about 100 kW. Put another way, the fraction of time the laser is emitting (the duty cycle) is 100 fs × 100 MHz = 10⁻⁵, so the peak is 10⁵ times the average. About 1 W mistakes the average power for the peak, and about 10 µW wrongly multiplies the average power by the duty cycle. For a sech²-shaped pulse a factor of 0.88 applies, giving about 88 kW. This high peak power is why ultrashort pulses are used for nonlinear optics and micromachining.

ultrafast-004.question: A pulse with a center wavelength of 1030 nm and a spectral width (FWHM) of 10 nm is measured to be 600 fs long. Which is closest to the shortest pulse duration obtainable by compensating dispersion without changing the spectrum? (Assume a Gaussian shape with a time-bandwidth product lower limit of ΔνΔt = 0.441; c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s.)
choices: About 160 fs
About 110 fs
About 600 fs
ultrafast-004.explanation: The frequency width is Δν = cΔλ/λ² = 3.0×10⁸ × 10×10⁻⁹ / (1030×10⁻⁹)² ≈ 2.8 THz. The transform-limited duration is 0.441 / (2.8×10¹²) ≈ 1.56×10⁻¹³ s, about 160 fs, and the product with the measured 600 fs, ΔνΔt ≈ 1.7, is about 4 times the lower limit. This shows that the pulse is chirped, with arrival times that differ by frequency, and applying dispersion of the opposite sign can shorten it to about 160 fs. About 110 fs uses the sech² factor of 0.315, which does not match the Gaussian assumption. Keeping about 600 fs assumes that pulse duration is set by spectral width alone; the time-bandwidth product is a lower limit, and equality holds only without chirp.

ultrafast-005.question: Which correctly describes what happens when a short, unchirped (transform-limited) light pulse passes through a glass plate with normal dispersion?
choices: Shorter-wavelength components travel faster, so short wavelengths lead and long ones trail, and the pulse shortens in time with a higher peak
The temporal shape is unchanged, while dispersion generates new frequency components so that only the spectrum broadens
Longer wavelengths travel faster, so they lead and shorter ones trail; the pulse broadens in time while the spectral shape is unchanged
ultrafast-005.explanation: In a medium with normal dispersion (group-velocity dispersion β₂ > 0, group delay dispersion GDD > 0), longer wavelengths have higher group velocity. The arrival times of the frequency components therefore spread, with long wavelengths (low frequencies) at the front and short wavelengths (high frequencies) at the back, giving an up-chirp in which the instantaneous frequency rises with time. An unchirped pulse, with all components in phase, is already in its shortest state, so dispersion broadens it and never shortens it. Dispersion is a linear effect that only changes the phase at each frequency, so the spectral shape is unchanged. Broadening the spectrum without changing the temporal shape is the signature of intensity-dependent self-phase modulation, which should be distinguished from dispersion.

ultrafast-006.question: A transform-limited Gaussian pulse with a duration of 20 fs (FWHM) at a center wavelength of 800 nm passes through 10 mm of fused silica with a group-velocity dispersion of 36 fs²/mm. Which is closest to the duration of the output pulse? (τ_out = τ₀√(1 + (4 ln2 × GDD/τ₀²)²); ignore higher-order dispersion.)
choices: About 20 fs
About 54 fs
About 70 fs
ultrafast-006.explanation: The group delay dispersion is GDD = 36 fs²/mm × 10 mm = 360 fs². Since 4 ln2 × 360 / 20² ≈ 2.50, τ_out = 20 × √(1 + 2.50²) ≈ 20 × 2.69 ≈ 54 fs, broadening by about 2.7 times. About 70 fs computes 20 × (1 + 2.50) without the square root. About 20 fs assumes that just 10 mm of glass has no effect. In the same glass a 100 fs pulse would become about 100.5 fs, almost unchanged, but because the effect scales as GDD/τ₀², shorter pulses broaden sharply. For pulses of a few tens of fs or shorter, even the dispersion of lenses and windows must be compensated.

ultrafast-007.question: Which optical system can be used to compress an up-chirped pulse produced by normal dispersion?
choices: A system that adds plates of the same glass to provide more positive group delay dispersion, so the short wavelengths catch up
A system that cuts out only the center of the spectrum with a narrow bandpass filter, removing the chirped wavelength components at both ends
A system such as a grating pair, prism pair or chirped mirrors giving negative group delay dispersion, so short wavelengths go through first
ultrafast-007.explanation: An up-chirped pulse has long wavelengths at the front and short wavelengths at the back. To compress it, negative GDD is applied to advance the lagging short-wavelength components and delay the long-wavelength ones. Grating pairs and prism pairs create negative GDD because the geometric path length changes with wavelength, and chirped mirrors do so because the depth of reflection in the multilayer changes with wavelength. Adding glass adds dispersion of the same sign, broadening the pulse further. Narrowing the spectrum with a bandpass filter actually lengthens the transform-limited duration because of the time-bandwidth lower limit, so no shorter pulse results.

ultrafast-008.question: In chirped-pulse amplification (CPA), what is the main purpose of stretching the pulse in time before amplification?
choices: To lower the peak power, avoiding nonlinear effects such as self-focusing in the amplifier and optical damage, then compress the pulse back after amplification
Stretching the pulse also broadens its spectrum, which makes full use of the amplifier's wide gain bandwidth out to its edges
A stretched pulse shortens naturally through gain saturation in the amplifier, so short pulses are obtained without a compressor
ultrafast-008.explanation: Amplifying a fs pulse directly would push the peak power to around 10 GW even at an energy of 1 mJ, so Kerr self-focusing and self-phase modulation would distort the waveform and damage the gain medium and mirrors. In CPA a stretcher such as a grating arrangement applies large dispersion to stretch the pulse by 10⁴, for example from 100 fs to 1 ns, lowering the peak power by the same factor before amplification, and finally a compressor with the opposite dispersion restores the original duration. Dispersion does not change the spectral shape, so stretching does not broaden the spectrum. Nor does the pulse shorten on its own in the amplifier; the compressor is essential. CPA made TW-class peak powers possible even with tabletop systems.

ultrafast-009.question: In one method, the spectrum is broadened by self-phase modulation in an optical fiber (or a gas-filled hollow-core fiber) and negative dispersion is then applied, giving a pulse shorter than the input pulse. Why does this method shorten the pulse?
choices: Self-phase modulation itself compresses the pulse in time, and the negative dispersion only undoes the broadening caused by positive dispersion during propagation
The spectrum broadened by self-phase modulation is nearly linearly chirped near the center, so aligning the phases with negative dispersion gives a shorter pulse
Self-phase modulation narrows the spectrum and raises the peak intensity, at which the absorption in the fiber saturates and trims the wings of the pulse
ultrafast-009.explanation: In self-phase modulation the phase changes in proportion to the intensity I(t), so the instantaneous frequency shifts, lower at the front of the pulse and higher at the back. New frequencies are generated and the spectrum broadens, but without dispersion the temporal shape does not change. Near the center the chirp is nearly proportional to time, so applying negative GDD with a prism pair or chirped mirrors brings the components of the broadened spectrum together in time, giving a short pulse close to the transform limit. The time compression happens at the dispersion-compensation stage, not in self-phase modulation itself. It is neither a spectral narrowing effect nor absorption saturation. Near the edges of the spectrum the chirp departs from linear, so a small pedestal remains after compression.

ultrafast-010.question: Which correctly describes measuring the duration of a pulse of about 100 fs by intensity autocorrelation using second-harmonic generation (SHG)?
choices: A photodetector is too slow, but the width of the autocorrelation trace equals the pulse duration directly, so no pulse shape needs to be assumed
Recording the second harmonic versus delay uniquely determines even the asymmetric shape of the pulse front and back and the sign of the chirp
The pulse is split in two with a delay, the second harmonic from their overlap is recorded versus delay, and the width is divided by a shape factor (√2 for a Gaussian)
ultrafast-010.explanation: Even the fastest photodetectors and oscilloscopes respond in a few ps at best, so a 100 fs pulse cannot be measured. Intensity autocorrelation uses the pulse itself as a gate: the delay τ between the two halves of the split pulse is varied while the strength of the second harmonic from a nonlinear crystal, ∫I(t)I(t − τ)dt, is recorded. The autocorrelation is wider than the pulse, by √2 times for a Gaussian and about 1.54 times for a sech² shape, so a shape is assumed for the conversion. For example, an autocorrelation width of 141 fs means about 100 fs for a Gaussian. The autocorrelation is always symmetric, so asymmetry of the pulse and the sign of the chirp cannot be determined; methods that also retrieve the phase, such as FROG, are needed for that.

ultrafast-011.question: An optical frequency comb has a repetition rate f_rep = 250 MHz and a carrier-envelope offset frequency f_ceo = 20 MHz. The beat frequency between a continuous-wave laser of unknown frequency and the comb mode with mode number n = 1.2×10⁶ is 30 MHz, and the laser frequency is known to be above that mode. Which is closest to the laser frequency? (fₙ = nf_rep + f_ceo)
ultrafast-011.explanation: Since 1.2×10⁶ × 250 MHz = 300 THz, the mode frequency is fₙ = 300 THz + 20 MHz = 300.000020 THz. The laser is 30 MHz above this mode, so it is at 300.000020 THz + 30 MHz = 300.000050 THz. 300.000030 THz forgets f_ceo, and 299.999990 THz takes the beat on the wrong side. The beat frequency alone cannot tell above from below, so in practice f_rep or another parameter is changed slightly and the sign is found from whether the beat rises or falls, while the mode number n is found from a coarse measurement with a wavemeter. If f_rep and f_ceo are locked to a microwave frequency standard, the optical frequency can be measured with that accuracy.

ultrafast-012.question: Each time a pulse makes one round trip of the cavity, the phase offset between the carrier and the envelope (the carrier-envelope phase) advances by Δφ = π/2. For a repetition rate of 100 MHz, which is closest to the offset frequency f_ceo? (f_ceo = (Δφ/2π) f_rep)
choices: 25 MHz
50 MHz
About 157 MHz
ultrafast-012.explanation: f_ceo = (π/2)/(2π) × 100 MHz = 100 MHz / 4 = 25 MHz. In the cavity, dispersion of the medium makes the phase velocity of the carrier differ from the group velocity of the envelope, so on each round trip the carrier crests slip by Δφ relative to the envelope peak. In the spectrum of the pulse train this slip corresponds to shifting every mode by f_ceo, giving fₙ = nf_rep + f_ceo. 50 MHz is the value for Δφ = π. About 157 MHz multiplies by Δφ ≈ 1.57 without dividing by 2π; because Δφ repeats every 2π, f_ceo is normally expressed as a value between 0 and f_rep, so it does not exceed 100 MHz. Δφ changes with temperature and pump power, so f_ceo is measured and controlled.

ultrafast-013.question: When f_ceo is measured by f-2f self-referencing, why must the comb spectrum span at least one octave (a range over which the frequency doubles)?
choices: With a one-octave spectrum the pulse becomes shorter than one optical cycle, so f_ceo is fixed at zero and easier to measure
The beat between the two modes at the ends of the octave becomes twice f_rep, so it can be distinguished from f_rep and read as f_ceo
The second harmonic 2fₙ of a low-side mode fₙ beats with the high-side mode f₂ₙ to give f_ceo, which requires components at both fₙ and 2fₙ
ultrafast-013.explanation: f_ceo is a shift common to all modes, so it cannot be obtained from beats between modes (integer multiples of f_rep). In the f-2f method, components on the low-frequency side of the spectrum are frequency-doubled in a nonlinear crystal and overlapped with modes on the high-frequency side of the original spectrum. Since 2(nf_rep + f_ceo) − (2nf_rep + f_ceo) = f_ceo, the beat gives f_ceo directly. This requires fₙ and 2fₙ to be in the same spectrum, that is, a bandwidth of at least one octave, usually achieved by broadening the spectrum in photonic crystal fiber or similar. Having an octave does not make f_ceo zero. Beats between modes contain no information about f_ceo.

ultrafast-014.question: In an optical frequency comb with a repetition rate f_rep = 250 MHz, f_rep changes by just 1 Hz while f_ceo is held constant. Which is closest to the change in frequency of a mode at about 300 THz (mode number n = 1.2×10⁶)?
choices: About 1.2 MHz
1 Hz
About 1.2 GHz
ultrafast-014.explanation: Since fₙ = nf_rep + f_ceo, with f_ceo constant Δfₙ = nΔf_rep = 1.2×10⁶ × 1 Hz = 1.2×10⁶ Hz, about 1.2 MHz. Because the mode number is large, a tiny change in f_rep is magnified, like a lever, in the optical frequency. 1 Hz assumes every mode moves by the same amount, which is what happens when f_ceo changes by 1 Hz. About 1.2 GHz is the value for Δf_rep = 1 kHz, a mix-up of units. The relative change Δf/f is nearly the same, 4×10⁻⁹, for f_rep and for the optical frequency, so determining optical frequencies precisely requires stabilizing f_rep with high accuracy or locking one of the modes to a stable optical reference.

ultrafast-015.question: For which pulses does the carrier-envelope phase (CEP) strongly affect experimental results? (Center wavelength 800 nm; one optical cycle is about 2.7 fs.)
choices: Long pulses with a FWHM of about 1 ns. The more oscillations within the envelope, the more the round-trip CEP slips accumulate and the more they matter
Pulses with a FWHM of about 5 fs, whose envelope holds only about two optical cycles. The peak field strength changes with the CEP
It is the same regardless of pulse duration; the CEP sets the pulse energy and intensity envelope shape, so it matters for every pulse
ultrafast-015.explanation: One cycle of 800 nm light is λ/c ≈ 2.7 fs, so the FWHM of a 5 fs pulse contains only about 1.9 cycles. With a CEP of 0 the carrier crest coincides with the envelope peak and the maximum field is large, while at π/2 the crest is offset and the maximum drops. Tunnel ionization, high-harmonic generation and attosecond pulse generation, which depend on the instantaneous field, are sensitive to this difference. A 100 fs pulse holds about 37 cycles, so changing the CEP hardly changes the maximum field, and for ns pulses it is completely negligible. The CEP is the phase of the carrier and does not change the pulse energy or the intensity envelope.

ultrafast-016.question: For a pulse of center frequency ω₀ passing through a dispersive medium, the spectral phase φ(ω) is expanded about ω₀. Which statement correctly describes how the terms of the expansion affect the position and shape of the pulse?
choices: The larger the first-order term (group delay), the more the pulse broadens, while the second-order term (group delay dispersion) only shifts the phase between carrier and envelope and leaves the pulse shape unchanged

The first-order term (group delay) only delays the whole pulse without changing its shape, while the second-order term (group delay dispersion) makes the delay differ with frequency and broadens the pulse

The zeroth- and first-order terms broaden the pulse, and second- and higher-order terms only change its arrival time, so however thick the glass, the pulse is only delayed and keeps its shape unchanged
ultrafast-016.explanation: Expanding φ(ω) = φ₀ + φ′(ω − ω₀) + φ″(ω − ω₀)²/2 + …, the zeroth-order term only changes the phase relation between carrier and envelope. The first-order coefficient φ′ is the group delay, which delays every frequency component equally, so the pulse is delayed without changing shape. The second-order coefficient φ″ is the group delay dispersion (GDD): because the group delay differs with frequency, the components arrive at different times, and the pulse becomes chirped and broadens. Third- and higher-order terms distort the shape asymmetrically. A large group delay by itself does not cause broadening; a pulse delayed by glass broadens because the group delay varies with frequency, that is, because there is GDD.

ultrafast-017.question: When a pulse stretched in a CPA system is compressed with a grating pair, setting the group delay dispersion (GDD) exactly to zero sometimes still fails to reach the transform-limited duration, leaving small pulses on one side of the main pulse. Which is the main cause?
choices: Residual third-order dispersion (curvature of group delay versus frequency) delays both ends of the spectrum in the same direction, giving an asymmetric shape with a tail or small pulses on one side
The GDD flips between positive and negative from one measurement to the next, so on average the pulse looks broad; offsetting the GDD slightly toward positive removes all of the small pulses
At zero GDD the carrier and envelope phases do not line up, so the carrier-envelope phase changes randomly from pulse to pulse, and averaged over many pulses the pulse looks broad
ultrafast-017.explanation: The group delay is τ(ω) = φ′(ω); the GDD is its slope and the third-order dispersion (TOD) its curvature. If TOD remains after the GDD is compensated, the group delay becomes a parabola about the center frequency, so components at both ends of the spectrum are delayed (or advanced) in the same direction; the temporal shape becomes asymmetric, with an oscillating tail or a train of small pulses on one side. The broader the spectrum, the larger the effect, so designs match the TOD of stretcher and compressor or compensate higher orders using prism-grating combinations or chirped mirrors. Shifting the GDD slightly cannot cancel a cubic phase, so the small pulses remain. The CEP is the relation between the field oscillation and the envelope and does not change the envelope width.

ultrafast-018.question: In ultrashort pulse measurement, why can FROG (frequency-resolved optical gating) obtain information that intensity autocorrelation cannot?
choices: Like autocorrelation it measures the second-harmonic power versus delay, but it records the temporal waveform directly with a fast detector, so the phase is also obtained
It measures only the pulse spectrum at high resolution and obtains the temporal waveform from its Fourier transform, so no delay optics are needed and the phase is also known
It records the spectrum of the gated signal at each delay to form a 2D image, from which an iterative algorithm retrieves the intensity and phase (chirp) of the pulse
ultrafast-018.explanation: Intensity autocorrelation is a one-dimensional signal versus delay τ; converting it to a duration requires assuming a pulse shape, and the phase information is lost. In FROG, two delayed copies of the pulse are overlapped in a nonlinear crystal as in autocorrelation, but the generated light is recorded as a spectrum by a spectrometer instead of being detected directly. The 2D image versus delay and frequency (a spectrogram) shows which frequencies are present at which times, so an iterative algorithm can retrieve intensity and phase almost uniquely. Second-harmonic FROG cannot distinguish only the direction of time. No detector is fast enough to record a femtosecond pulse directly, and the spectral intensity alone does not give the phase, so its Fourier transform does not determine the temporal waveform.

ultrafast-019.question: In a pump-probe experiment, a corner cube (a reflector that returns light parallel to its incoming direction) in the probe path is moved along the incident beam direction to vary the delay. Which value is closest to the change in delay when the corner cube is moved by 15 µm? Assume air and c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s.
choices: About 50 fs
About 100 fs
About 200 fs
ultrafast-019.explanation: Moving the reflector by Δx changes the path on both the way in and the way out, so the optical path changes by 2Δx = 30 µm. The delay change is 2Δx/c = 30×10⁻⁶ m / 3.0×10⁸ m/s = 1.0×10⁻¹³ s, about 100 fs. About 50 fs uses Δx/c without the round trip, and about 200 fs doubles the round-trip factor again. Since 1 µm of travel corresponds to about 6.7 fs of delay, stepping the delay in increments of a few femtoseconds requires a stage positioned to about 0.1 µm. The time resolution of the measurement, however, is set not by the delay step but by the pump and probe pulse durations (their cross-correlation width).

ultrafast-020.question: Dual-comb spectroscopy is performed with one comb at a repetition rate f_rep = 100 MHz and another whose repetition rate is higher by Δf_rep = 1 kHz. When the light of the two combs is combined and detected, the optical bandwidth is compressed by a factor f_rep/Δf_rep into the electrical signal band. Under the condition that the electrical bandwidth must not exceed f_rep/2 (so that aliased copies do not overlap), which value is closest to the maximum optical bandwidth that can be measured?
choices: About 5 THz
About 10 THz
About 50 MHz
ultrafast-020.explanation: An optical bandwidth B_opt maps to B_opt × Δf_rep/f_rep in the electrical signal. This must not exceed f_rep/2 = 50 MHz, so B_opt ≤ (f_rep/2)(f_rep/Δf_rep) = 50 MHz × 10⁵ = 5×10¹² Hz, about 5 THz. About 10 THz drops the 1/2 in f_rep/2, and about 50 MHz forgets the compression factor, taking the electrical bandwidth as the optical one. A smaller Δf_rep allows a wider bandwidth, but the time to acquire one spectrum, 1/Δf_rep (1 ms here), becomes longer, so bandwidth trades off against measurement speed. The technique can be viewed as Fourier-transform spectroscopy without a moving mirror, with each mode frequency known to the accuracy of the comb.

ultrafast-021.question: In a chirped-pulse amplifier, an 800 nm pulse passes through 1 cm of a crystal with nonlinear index n₂ = 3×10⁻²⁰ m²/W at a peak intensity of 10 GW/cm². Which value is closest to the nonlinear phase from self-phase modulation (the B-integral) B = (2π/λ)n₂IL? (Take the intensity as constant along the length.)
choices: About 0.04 rad
About 0.24 rad
About 24 rad
ultrafast-021.explanation: 10 GW/cm² = 1×10¹⁴ W/m², so B = (2π/8×10⁻⁷ m) × 3×10⁻²⁰ m²/W × 1×10¹⁴ W/m² × 0.01 m ≈ 0.24 rad. About 0.04 rad omits the factor 2π, and about 24 rad comes from a factor-of-100 slip in converting W/cm² to W/m² (a factor of 10⁴). The B-integral is summed over the whole amplifier path, and once it exceeds roughly 1 rad, spectral distortion from self-phase modulation and the growth of intensity ripples in the beam by self-focusing become noticeable, degrading the compressed pulse or damaging optics. Stretching the pulse in CPA to lower its peak intensity is a way to keep B small.

ultrafast-022.question: Drilling metal with femtosecond laser pulses leaves less melting around the hole and fewer heat effects than nanosecond pulses. Which is the main reason?
choices: The pulse is shorter than electron-to-lattice heat transfer (about a ps), so only the irradiated region heats and is ejected before heat spreads
The pulse energy is small, so the metal barely heats, and machining proceeds entirely through photochemical reactions in which light breaks atomic bonds directly
A short pulse has a broad spectrum that metals absorb poorly, so most of the light reflects from the surface and only the small remainder drills the hole
ultrafast-022.explanation: Light absorbed in a metal first gives its energy to the electrons, which pass it to the lattice through electron–phonon coupling over about a picosecond; heat conduction then spreads it outward. With nanosecond pulses, heat spreads during the pulse, leaving a large melted layer and heat-affected zone. With femtosecond pulses, only a thin irradiated layer becomes extremely hot and dense and is ejected before energy spreads, giving clean-edged micromachining. Machining needs high peak intensity, so it is not true that the temperature barely rises. A broad spectrum hardly changes metal absorption, and losing light to reflection does not explain the small heat effects.

ultrafast-023.question: In a 4f pulse shaper, an ultrashort pulse is spread spatially by wavelength using a grating and lens, a liquid-crystal spatial light modulator is placed in the lens's focal plane, and a second lens and grating recombine the light. Which correctly describes what this device does?
choices: In the focal plane, position corresponds to time within the pulse, so changing the transmission of each pixel cuts out part of the pulse in time and shortens it
The spatial light modulator adds new frequency components to the spectrum and broadens it, so the pulse can be made shorter than the Fourier-transform limit of the input pulse

In the focal plane, position corresponds to optical frequency, so changing the phase (or amplitude) of each pixel imposes any spectral phase, allowing chirp compensation and desired temporal waveforms
ultrafast-023.explanation: The grating sends each frequency in a different direction, and the lens lines them up in its focal plane, so focal-plane position corresponds to optical frequency. Changing the phase at each pixel of the liquid-crystal modulator there gives each spectral component any phase, so residual dispersion can be compensated and pulse trains, chirped waveforms and other desired temporal shapes synthesized. The second lens and grating recombine the light into one beam. Treating position as time confuses the spectral plane with the time domain. Liquid-crystal changes in phase or transmission create no new frequencies, so the spectrum does not broaden and the pulse cannot be made shorter than the transform limit.

ultrafast-024.question: In a BBO crystal, the 400 nm second harmonic is generated from an 800 nm fundamental. If the delay between the two waves due to their group-velocity difference (group-velocity mismatch) is 0.2 ps per mm of crystal, which crystal thickness makes the separation of the two pulses at the exit equal to the pulse width for a 50 fs fundamental?
choices: About 4 mm
About 2.5 mm
About 0.25 mm
ultrafast-024.explanation: The pulses separate by 200 fs per mm, so a 50 fs separation needs 50/200 = 0.25 mm. About 4 mm divides 0.2 ps by 0.05 ps, inverting the ratio. About 2.5 mm comes from a slip in converting fs and ps. In a thicker crystal the fundamental and second-harmonic pulses walk apart as they travel, so the second-harmonic pulse stretches in time and the conversion efficiency levels off. Seen another way, a thick crystal has a narrow phase-matching bandwidth and cannot convert the broad spectrum of a short pulse. Femtosecond frequency conversion therefore uses thin crystals, balancing efficiency against bandwidth.

ultrafast-025.question: When intense femtosecond pulses are focused into a noble gas, odd harmonics of the fundamental extend to tens of orders or more (high-harmonic generation). Which statement correctly explains this?
choices: It comes from high-order terms in a perturbative expansion of the atomic nonlinear polarization; intensity drops steeply with order, and even and odd harmonics alternate with equal strength
Tunnel-ionized electrons return to the parent ion and recombine, emitting light every half cycle, so only odd harmonics appear; it is a source of attosecond pulses
It is stimulated Raman scattering from molecular vibrations, giving Stokes lines spaced by the Raman shift, and they appear with equal strength up to tens of orders regardless of pulse intensity
ultrafast-025.explanation: High harmonics arise when the field is comparable to the atomic binding field. The electron tunnels out, is driven back to the parent ion when the field reverses, and recombines, emitting a photon whose energy is its kinetic energy plus the ionization energy. This repeats every half cycle with alternating direction, so only odd harmonics appear, with a flat plateau of nearly constant strength that ends abruptly at a cutoff order. The short bursts every half cycle form a train of attosecond pulses, and single-cycle driving pulses can produce an isolated attosecond pulse. High-order perturbative terms fall steeply with order and cannot explain the plateau, and symmetric atoms produce no even harmonics. Raman scattering shifts light by vibrational frequencies and does not produce harmonics.

ultrafast-026.question: A pulse with 1 mJ energy and 50 fs duration is focused to a Gaussian beam radius w = 10 µm (the radius at which the intensity is 1/e² of the center value). Which value is closest to the peak intensity at the center of the focus, I = 2P/(πw²), where P is the peak power and the pulse is treated as a 50 fs rectangle?
choices: About 1.3×10¹⁶ W/cm²
About 6.4×10¹⁵ W/cm²
About 1.3×10²⁰ W/cm²
ultrafast-026.explanation: The peak power is P = 1×10⁻³ J/50×10⁻¹⁵ s = 2×10¹⁰ W. With w = 10 µm = 1.0×10⁻³ cm, πw² ≈ 3.14×10⁻⁶ cm², so I = 2 × 2×10¹⁰/3.14×10⁻⁶ ≈ 1.3×10¹⁶ W/cm². About 6.4×10¹⁵ W/cm² drops the factor 2 by which the center intensity of a Gaussian beam exceeds the average. About 1.3×10²⁰ W/cm² is the value computed in W/m² but labeled per cm², 10⁴ times too large. Above roughly 10¹⁴ W/cm² even gas atoms are ionized by the strong field, so focusing at this intensity in air creates a plasma, and high-intensity experiments are done in vacuum.

ultrafast-027.question: An ultrashort pulse is split in two, one copy is delayed by τ = 0.50 ps, and the two are recombined and measured with a spectrometer; periodic fringes appear in the spectrum. Which value is closest to the fringe spacing in wavelength near the 800 nm center wavelength? (Take the fringe spacing in frequency as 1/τ; c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s.)
choices: About 2.1 nm
About 8.5 nm
About 4.3 nm
ultrafast-027.explanation: The spectrum of the sum of two pulses separated by τ is 2|E(ω)|²[1 + cos(ωτ)], so fringes appear at a frequency spacing of Δν = 1/τ = 1/(0.50 ps) = 2.0 THz. In wavelength, Δλ = λ²Δν/c = (800×10⁻⁹)² × 2.0×10¹²/3.0×10⁸ ≈ 4.3×10⁻⁹ m, about 4.3 nm. About 2.1 nm takes Δν as 1/(2τ), and about 8.5 nm takes it as 2/τ. The longer the delay, the finer the fringes, and they vanish once they become finer than the spectrometer's resolution. Because the fringe positions are set by the spectral phase difference between the two pulses, this interference is the basis of spectral interferometry and SPIDER, which measure the phase of a pulse.

ultrafast-028.question: Which statement correctly describes the operation of a regenerative amplifier, used to amplify femtosecond oscillator pulses (around a nanojoule) to the millijoule level?
choices: Every oscillator pulse passes through the gain medium once, so the repetition rate stays at the oscillator's tens of megahertz and only the energy rises
A Pockels cell and a polarizer select one pulse and trap it in a cavity, where it makes more than ten round trips before being switched out, so the repetition rate falls to the kilohertz range
Pulses are overlapped inside the gain medium and merged into one, so the energies of many oscillator pulses add up and the pulse also becomes shorter
ultrafast-028.explanation: A single pass gives too little gain, so a regenerative amplifier uses a Pockels cell, which switches polarization with a voltage, together with a polarizer as an optical switch to pick one pulse from the oscillator train and admit it to a cavity. The pulse makes a dozen or so round trips through the gain medium, is amplified by roughly 10⁶, and is switched out again when the gain saturates. Because the energy stored in the gain medium goes into one pulse, the repetition rate drops to the kilohertz range set by the pumping and the switch. Amplifying at the oscillator's repetition rate to millijoules would need tens of kilowatts of average power, which is not practical. The amplifier does not merge pulses; it is combined with CPA so that the pulse is stretched before amplification.

ultrafast-029.question: In chirped-pulse amplification, when the gain of a Ti:sapphire amplifier is made very large, for example 10⁷, the amplified pulse may come out longer than the oscillator pulse even after compression. Which combination of main cause and remedy is correct?
choices: Raising the pulse energy raises the lower limit of the time–bandwidth product, so higher-energy pulses cannot be made as short, and nothing can be done about it
The dispersion added by the stretcher is cancelled inside the amplifier and the pulse shortens, so the compressor overcompresses it; reducing the stretcher's dispersion prevents this

Gain narrowing, in which the center of the gain spectrum is amplified more strongly and the spectrum narrows, is the cause; it is countered by shaping the spectrum, for example with filters that flatten the gain peak
ultrafast-029.explanation: The amplifier's gain peaks at certain wavelengths, and when many passes build up a large total gain, the gain difference between the center and the wings is multiplied up. The amplified spectrum therefore comes out narrower than the input (gain narrowing), the transform-limited pulse duration grows, and compression cannot restore the original shortness. Remedies include filters that slightly suppress the center of the gain peak, shaping the input spectrum in advance, and using optical parametric amplification, which shows little gain narrowing. The lower limit of the time–bandwidth product does not depend on energy; it is set by the spectral width. Dispersion is not cancelled by amplification; the stretcher and compressor are matched to each other.

ultrafast-030.question: Off-axis parabolic mirrors rather than lenses are often used to focus ultrashort pulses of a few to a few tens of femtoseconds. Which is the main reason?
choices: Reflection involves no glass, so there is no dispersion or chromatic aberration, and a paraboloid focuses collimated light to a point without aberration
A parabolic mirror reverses the phase of the light at the focus and compresses the pulse in time, so it compensates the chirp while focusing
Lenses always break when the intensity is too high, but mirrors have damage thresholds orders of magnitude higher than glass and can be used at any intensity
ultrafast-030.explanation: Passing through a lens broadens the pulse through the glass's group-delay dispersion, chromatic aberration shifts the focus with wavelength, and because the glass thickness differs between the center and edge of the lens, the pulse front lags the wavefront; together these lengthen the pulse at the focus. Reflection from a metal or dielectric-coated mirror involves no travel through material, so none of these occur. A spherical mirror used at an angle shows astigmatism, so an off-axis section of a paraboloid is used, which focuses collimated light to a point without aberration. Reflection only changes the phase uniformly and cannot compensate chirp. Mirror coatings also have damage thresholds, so they cannot be used at any intensity.

ultrafast-031.question: When an 800 nm pulse passes through a fused-silica plate, the carrier travels at the phase velocity c/n and the envelope at the group velocity c/n_g, so the carrier-envelope phase (CEP) shifts. With refractive index n = 1.4533 and group index n_g = 1.4671, which value is closest to the plate thickness L = λ/(n_g − n) that shifts the CEP by 2π?
choices: About 0.55 µm
About 58 µm
About 29 µm
ultrafast-031.explanation: n_g − n = 1.4671 − 1.4533 = 0.0138, so L = 0.800 µm/0.0138 ≈ 58 µm. Over a thickness L the envelope falls behind the carrier by (n_g − n)L/c, shifting the CEP by 2π(n_g − n)L/λ. About 29 µm is the thickness for a shift of π. About 0.55 µm is the wavelength in the medium, λ/n, which ignores the difference between group and phase velocity. Because a few tens of micrometers of glass shift the CEP by a full cycle, few-cycle pulses have their CEP fine-tuned by sliding a pair of glass wedges to change the thickness traversed. In a normally dispersive material n_g > n, so the envelope lags behind the carrier.

ultrafast-032.question: When an ultrashort pulse is split into two copies that are recombined collinearly and the second-harmonic intensity is measured as the delay is varied, an interferometric autocorrelation with fringes oscillating at the optical period is obtained. For an unchirped pulse, which is the correct ratio of the peak at zero delay to the background at large delay?
choices: 1 to 1: at zero delay the signal equals the background and only the fringe oscillation appears
3 to 1: the same ratio as the fringe-free intensity autocorrelation
8 to 1: larger than the 3 to 1 of the fringe-averaged intensity autocorrelation
ultrafast-032.explanation: When the fields E(t) and E(t − τ) are superposed collinearly, the second-harmonic intensity is the square of the square of the total field, that is, proportional to its fourth power. At zero delay the field doubles, so the signal rises by 2⁴ = 16; at large delay, where the pulses do not overlap, it is the sum of the second harmonics generated by each pulse, a factor of 2. The ratio is therefore 16 to 2, or 8 to 1. The fringe-averaged intensity autocorrelation in a collinear setup gives 3 to 1. With chirp the fringes die out sooner away from zero delay, so the 8-to-1 ratio and the fringe shape serve as a guide when adjusting pulse compression. One to one overlooks the interference between the fields of the two pulses.

ultrafast-033.question: Which correctly describes nonlinear polarization evolution (NPE), used for passive mode locking of fiber lasers?
choices: Via the Kerr effect, elliptically polarized light rotates its polarization by an intensity-dependent amount, so stronger peaks pass the polarizer better, like a saturable absorber
Stronger light cancels the fiber birefringence and keeps its polarization unchanged, so it passes the polarizer less, and only weak light grows, shortening the pulse
The polarization rotation depends only on fiber length, not intensity, so the polarizer orientation keeps the cavity loss constant and locks the longitudinal-mode phases
ultrafast-033.explanation: As elliptically polarized light travels through a fiber, the Kerr-induced nonlinear phase differs between the two polarization components, so the orientation of the polarization ellipse rotates by an amount that depends on intensity. If the polarizer and wave plates are set so that more intense light passes the polarizer more easily, the pulse peak sees low loss while the wings and weak light see high loss. This is the action of a fast saturable absorber, and over many round trips a short, intense pulse is selected. Using no absorbing material, it resists damage and responds quickly, but changes in birefringence with temperature or bending can shift the operating point. If stronger light suffered more loss, no pulse would build up. The intensity dependence of the rotation is the essence of the scheme.

ultrafast-034.question: A chirped mirror, used to compensate dispersion of ultrashort pulses, is a dielectric multilayer whose layer thicknesses change gradually with depth. Which correctly describes how it provides negative group-delay dispersion?
choices: Stacked metal films make the absorption wavelength dependent, absorbing short wavelengths strongly at the surface and reflecting only the delayed long wavelengths
The layer period grows with depth, so longer wavelengths are reflected by deeper layers and delayed, and the short wavelengths return first
Grooves etched in the surface diffract each wavelength at a different angle, sending shorter wavelengths along longer paths to delay them
ultrafast-034.explanation: A quarter-wave multilayer strongly reflects the wavelength matched to its layer period. In a chirped mirror the period is short near the surface and longer deeper down, so short wavelengths are reflected by shallow layers and long wavelengths penetrate deeper before being reflected. The longer round-trip path delays the long wavelengths, so the short wavelengths come back first, which is negative group-delay dispersion that cancels the up-chirp from normal dispersion. One bounce gives only a small amount of dispersion, so several bounces are used to set the total. Careful design of the layer thicknesses can compensate higher-order dispersion as well, and mirrors are sometimes used in matched pairs to suppress oscillations in the group delay. The mirror relies neither on absorption nor on diffraction from surface grooves.

ultrafast-035.question: When an ultrashort pulse acquires angular dispersion (different wavelengths travel in different directions) from a grating or prism, its arrival time varies across the beam cross section. Which explains this correctly?
choices: The phase fronts (wavefronts) tilt relative to the propagation direction, but the pulse front stays parallel to them, so the arrival time is the same everywhere
The pulse arrives later at the center of the beam and earlier at the edge, curving the pulse front like a lens and shifting the focus back and forth
The pulse front (joining the envelope peaks) tilts relative to the wavefront, so one side of the beam arrives before the other
ultrafast-035.explanation: With angular dispersion, components traveling in slightly different directions for each wavelength overlap, and the pulse front joining the envelope peaks tilts relative to the wavefront. The tilt angle γ is given by tanγ = λ dθ/dλ and is proportional to the angular dispersion dθ/dλ. One side of the beam arrives before the other, so on focusing the pulse lengthens and the timing varies across the sample. With a grating or prism pair aligned parallel and passed twice (double pass), both the angular dispersion and the spatial chirp cancel, and no tilt remains. The tilt is also used deliberately, for example to phase-match terahertz generation. A curved pulse front arises from other causes such as lens chromatic aberration, not from angular dispersion.

ultrafast-036.question: A mode-locked laser with a 1.875 m linear cavity emits pulses with a center wavelength of 800 nm and a spectral width (FWHM) of 10 nm. Which value is closest to the number of longitudinal modes within the spectral width (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)?
choices: About 5.9×10⁴
About 2.9×10⁴
About 3.8×10⁸
ultrafast-036.explanation: The longitudinal mode spacing is f_rep = c/(2L) = 3.0×10⁸/(2 × 1.875) = 80 MHz. Converting the spectral width to frequency, Δν = cΔλ/λ² = 3.0×10⁸ × 10×10⁻⁹/(800×10⁻⁹)² ≈ 4.7 THz, so the number of modes is 4.7×10¹²/8.0×10⁷ ≈ 5.9×10⁴. About 2.9×10⁴ takes the mode spacing as c/L = 160 MHz, ignoring the round trip. About 3.8×10⁸ wrongly takes the frequency width as c/Δλ; a wavelength width is converted to a frequency width through λ²/c. With tens of thousands of modes locked in phase, short pulses of about 100 fs, set by the time–bandwidth product, follow one another every round-trip time (12.5 ns).

ultrafast-037.question: In chirped pulse amplification, a compressed pulse of 1.0 J is reflected from the final diffraction grating. To avoid damaging the grating, the fluence over the beam cross-section must be at most 0.20 J/cm². For a circular beam of uniform intensity (flat-top), which value is closest to the minimum beam diameter required?
choices: About 1.3 cm
About 2.2 cm
About 2.5 cm
ultrafast-037.explanation: The required area is 1.0 J/(0.20 J/cm²) = 5.0 cm², so the diameter is D = 2√(5.0/π) ≈ 2.5 cm. About 1.3 cm takes the radius √(5.0/π) as the diameter, and about 2.2 cm sets D² = 5.0 cm², dropping the π/4 in the area of a circle. In practice the beam strikes the grating obliquely, which spreads the illuminated area, and a Gaussian beam has a central fluence twice the average, so more margin is taken. Compressed pulses are short and damage components easily, so petawatt-class lasers use beams tens of cm in diameter and meter-scale gratings. Even in chirped pulse amplification, which stretches pulses before amplifying them, the final compressor can set the upper limit of the output.

ultrafast-038.question: Which correctly describes the principle of a streak camera, which measures the time variation of light such as fluorescence with ps resolution?
choices: The light is mixed with a delayed gate pulse in a nonlinear crystal, and the sum-frequency intensity is recorded as a function of delay
A photocathode converts the light into electrons, which a time-varying voltage deflects so that arrival time becomes position on a phosphor screen
The output of a fast photodiode is recorded directly on a wideband oscilloscope, and the variation is found from the rise of the waveform
ultrafast-038.explanation: In a streak camera, light passing a slit strikes a photocathode and produces photoelectrons; as the accelerated electrons pass between deflection electrodes, a rapidly changing voltage (the sweep) is applied. Electrons arriving earlier and later are deflected at different angles, so time is converted into position on the phosphor screen and recorded as a bright streak. The other axis can record position along the slit, or wavelength from a spectrograph placed in front, so a time-resolved spectrum is obtained in one shot. Measuring the sum frequency as a function of delay is the upconversion method, whose resolution is set by the gate pulse width. A photodiode and oscilloscope respond in a few ps at best and cannot reach below 1 ps.

ultrafast-039.question: In a solid-state laser passively mode-locked with a semiconductor saturable absorber mirror (SESAM), reducing the pump power led to a state in which the pulse-train amplitude is strongly modulated with a period of about µs (Q-switched mode locking). Which correctly gives the cause and the remedy?
choices: The pulse energy is too small to saturate the absorber well; lower the repetition rate or focus more tightly on the SESAM
The pulse energy is so large that the absorber is oversaturated; focus less tightly on the SESAM to reduce the degree of saturation
The cavity dispersion turned positive and broadened the pulses; compensating it with a prism pair makes operation stable regardless of pump power
ultrafast-039.explanation: In solid-state gain media with long upper-level lifetimes, pulse-energy fluctuations are only weakly restored, so relaxation oscillations tend to persist. A saturable absorber lowers the loss for stronger pulses, which amplifies these fluctuations. If the pulse energy is large enough compared with the saturation energies of the gain medium and absorber, gain saturation suppresses the fluctuations and gives continuous mode locking; if it is small, a Q-switched envelope appears. Remedies are therefore to pump harder, lengthen the cavity to lower the repetition rate and raise the energy per pulse, make the beam on the SESAM smaller so it saturates more easily, or choose an absorber with a smaller modulation depth. Focusing less tightly makes saturation harder and has the opposite effect. Dispersion sets the pulse width but is not the main cause of this instability.

ultrafast-040.question: Which correctly describes OPCPA, in which a stretched seed is amplified by optical parametric amplification in a nonlinear crystal pumped by intense short pulses, compared with chirped pulse amplification in a laser medium such as Ti:sapphire?
choices: The crystal can store the pump energy, so the arrival times of the pump and seed pulses do not need to be synchronized
The gain bandwidth is set by the fluorescence width of the laser medium, so it is narrower than in Ti:sapphire and unsuited to short pulses
No energy is stored and the idler carries off the energy difference, so heating is small and the gain band is broad
ultrafast-040.explanation: In optical parametric amplification, the seed is amplified as each pump photon splits into a signal (seed) photon and an idler photon. No energy is stored in energy levels, and the energy difference leaves as the idler, so little heat remains in the crystal and thermal lensing is minor. The gain bandwidth is set by phase matching and can be made very broad, for example with a noncollinear geometry, so even few-cycle pulses can be amplified. On the other hand, gain exists only while the pump is present, so the pump and seed must be synchronized to within about a ps or better. In return, light outside the pump window is not amplified, giving little light before and after the main pulse (high temporal contrast). A gain bandwidth set by the fluorescence width applies to amplification in laser media.

ultrafast-041.question: Active mode locking places an acousto-optic modulator or similar device in the cavity and varies the loss periodically at the round-trip frequency c/(2L). Which statement about it is correct?
choices: The modulation frequency can be chosen independently of the round-trip frequency, and the faster the modulation, the shorter the fs pulses obtained compared with passive mode locking by a saturable absorber

The sidebands created by the modulation overlap the neighboring longitudinal modes and lock their phases, and light gathers at the time of minimum loss, but the pulse width usually tends to stay at around ps
Because the loss is varied by an external signal, the modulation frequency need not be readjusted even when the cavity length changes with temperature, so it runs stably for a long time
ultrafast-041.explanation: Modulating the loss of one longitudinal mode at frequency f_m creates sidebands at ±f_m on either side. If f_m is matched to the mode spacing c/(2L), the sidebands overlap the neighboring modes and pull their phases, all mode phases line up, and a pulse forms at the time of minimum loss. However, the loss changes slowly compared with the pulse, and the shorter the pulse becomes, the less it shrinks per round trip, so the pulse width often settles at around a picosecond. A saturable absorber, which responds quickly to the pulse's own intensity, more easily gives short pulses, and the modulation frequency cannot be chosen independently of the round trip. If the cavity length drifts, synchronization breaks down, so the length or the modulation frequency is kept matched.

ultrafast-042.question: A Gires–Tournois interferometer (GTI) is a mirror built as a cavity of a thin air gap or glass plate whose back mirror is nearly 100% reflective and whose front is partially reflective; it is used to compensate the dispersion of ultrashort pulses. Which property of this mirror is correct?
choices: Its reflectance is nearly 100% at all wavelengths, but near resonance the reflection phase varies strongly with frequency, giving group-delay dispersion tunable by the spacing
Like a Fabry–Perot interferometer, it strongly transmits and removes light only at resonant wavelengths and reflects only light outside that band, giving the reflected light dispersion

Its reflection phase is constant with frequency, and only the material dispersion of the thick glass in front of the back mirror gives negative group-delay dispersion, so the value does not depend on the spacing
ultrafast-042.explanation: Because the back of a GTI is nearly totally reflective, all the light that enters is eventually reflected back, and the reflectance is nearly 1 (100%) at every wavelength. Meanwhile, light that makes more round trips inside the cavity before leaving is delayed more, so near resonance the reflection phase changes strongly with frequency, the group delay varies with frequency, and group-delay dispersion results. Its size is roughly proportional to the square of the spacing and can be adjusted by changing the spacing. However, the phase variation repeats every resonance period (free spectral range), so the usable bandwidth is limited. Removing light by transmission is the action of a Fabry–Perot interferometer whose back is also partially reflective. The material dispersion of glass is normal dispersion in the visible to near infrared and does not give negative dispersion.

ultrafast-043.question: In a pump-probe experiment, the pump (pulse width 100 fs) and probe (50 fs) are both unchirped Gaussian pulses. Which value is closest to the width of the cross-correlation of the two pulses, √(τ_pump² + τ_probe²) (all widths FWHM), which serves as a guide to the time resolution?
choices: About 150 fs
About 50 fs
About 112 fs
ultrafast-043.explanation: √(100² + 50²) = √12500 ≈ 112 fs. The signal measured in a pump-probe experiment is the sample response convolved with the cross-correlation of pump and probe, and the width of a convolution of Gaussians is the square root of the sum of squares. About 150 fs simply adds the two widths, a large overestimate for Gaussians. About 50 fs wrongly assumes the shorter pulse alone sets the resolution, overlooking that the longer pulse blurs the excitation time. To improve resolution, both pulses are shortened, and the dispersion of windows and lenses is compensated so the pulses are unchirped at the sample.

ultrafast-044.question: Continuous-wave light is coupled into a silicon-nitride ring resonator of radius 100 µm, and a microcomb is generated by four-wave mixing. If the waveguide's effective index is 1.8 and its group index 2.0, which value is closest to the comb line spacing (the resonator's free spectral range FSR = c/(n_g × circumference), c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)?
choices: About 240 GHz
About 265 GHz
About 1.5 THz
ultrafast-044.explanation: The circumference is 2π × 100 µm ≈ 628 µm, so FSR = 3.0×10⁸ / (2.0 × 6.28×10⁻⁴) ≈ 2.39×10¹¹ Hz, about 240 GHz. The spacing between neighboring resonances is set by how fast the phase changes with frequency, so the group index is used rather than the phase index. About 265 GHz is calculated with the effective index of 1.8. About 1.5 THz uses the 100 µm radius as the circumference. Line spacings of microresonator combs range from tens of GHz to THz, much larger than the f_rep of mode-locked lasers; individual lines are easy to separate with a spectrometer, but if the spacing is too large it cannot be measured directly with a photodetector, so the resonator size is chosen to suit the application.

ultrafast-045.question: A line of an optical frequency comb is locked to stable continuous-wave light at 300 THz (such as an optical-clock laser), and the comb's pulse train is detected to extract a 10 GHz microwave (optical frequency division). If the optical phase fluctuations are transferred divided by the frequency ratio N = 300 THz/10 GHz, by how many dB is the spectral density of the microwave's phase noise smaller than that of the light (phase noise is proportional to the square of the phase fluctuation)?
choices: About 45 dB
About 90 dB
No change (0 dB)
ultrafast-045.explanation: N = 300 THz/10 GHz = 3×10⁴; the phase fluctuations become 1/N, and the spectral density of phase noise, proportional to their square, becomes 1/N². Since 20 log₁₀(3×10⁴) ≈ 89.5 dB, it is about 90 dB smaller. About 45 dB is 10 log₁₀N, treating the ratio of the phase fluctuation amplitudes like a power ratio and dropping the square. Dividing the frequency keeps the timing fluctuation (time jitter) the same while the fluctuation expressed as phase shrinks in proportion to frequency, so saying it does not change is wrong. Microwaves made this way have far lower phase noise than electronic oscillators and are used in radar and precise time comparison.
